ui.header.subtitle: {filetype} · {size} · {tags}
ui.value.from_offset_tag: UTC{offset}  (from the camera's own offset tag)
ui.value.stationary: stationary at the moment of capture

ui.value.regions.one: {count} face region recorded by the camera or a photo app
ui.value.regions.other: {count} face regions recorded by the camera or a photo app

verdict.originality.unknown.label: UNKNOWN
verdict.originality.unknown.summary: Nothing in this file records a camera or a capture time, so there is no original to verify.
verdict.originality.good.label: ORIGINAL
verdict.originality.good.summary: Everything is consistent with a file straight off the camera.
verdict.originality.fair.label: LIKELY ORIGINAL
verdict.originality.fair.summary: Looks original, with small inconsistencies worth a glance.
verdict.originality.poor.label: MODIFIED
verdict.originality.poor.summary: This file has been edited or re-saved since it was taken.
verdict.originality.bad.label: INCONSISTENT
verdict.originality.bad.summary: The metadata contradicts itself — treat its claims with suspicion.
verdict.originality.reason.clean: No signs of editing or re-encoding.
verdict.originality.reason.nothing: No camera identity and no capture timestamp to reason about.
verdict.privacy.good.label: CLEAN
verdict.privacy.good.summary_empty: Nothing in this file identifies you, your device, or where you were.
verdict.privacy.good.summary_stripped: This file carries almost no metadata, so there is nothing to leak.
verdict.privacy.fair.label: LOW EXPOSURE
verdict.privacy.fair.summary: A few details leak, none of them pinpointing.
verdict.privacy.poor.label: MODERATE EXPOSURE
verdict.privacy.poor.summary: This file gives away more than most people expect.
verdict.privacy.bad.label: HIGH EXPOSURE
verdict.privacy.bad.summary: Sharing this file as-is hands over your location, device, or identity.
verdict.structure.good.label: CLEAN
verdict.structure.good.summary: The file structure is exactly what a normal image looks like.
verdict.structure.fair.label: MINOR ANOMALIES
verdict.structure.fair.summary: Small structural oddities, most likely harmless.
verdict.structure.poor.label: SUSPICIOUS
verdict.structure.poor.summary: This file contains things a plain photo should not.
verdict.structure.bad.label: HIGH RISK
verdict.structure.bad.summary: Do not open or forward this file until you know what is in it.
tag.creator: Creator
tag.title: Title
source_type.trainedalgorithmicmedia: Created by a generative AI model
source_type.compositewithtrainedalgorith: A composite that includes AI-generated elements
source_type.algorithmicallyenhanced: Algorithmically enhanced (e.g. AI upscaling or retouching)
source_type.minorhumanedits: Digitally captured with minor human edits
source_type.softwareimage: Generated by software (e.g. a screenshot or render)
source_type.virtualrecording: A recording of a virtual scene
filename_note.apple: iPhone and iPad cameras name files this way.
filename_note.pixel: Pixel camera app naming, used since Android 11.
filename_note.camera: Standard naming used by most dedicated cameras.
filename_note.screenshot: The filename says this is a screen capture, not a photo.
filename_note.telegram: Telegram names saved photos this way.
filename_note.messaging: A generic name several messengers use when saving.
filename_note.email: A generic name used when saving an attachment.
finding.authenticity.editor_software.tit: This file was last written by {editor}, not by a camera
finding.authenticity.editor_software.det: The Software tag says {editor} saved this file. That application edits pixels, so the image you are looking at is not what the sensor recorded.
The Software tag says {editor} saved this file. That does not prove the picture was altered, but the file has certainly been through another program since it was taken.

finding.authenticity.xmp_history.title.one: The file carries an edit history with {count} recorded step
finding.authenticity.xmp_history.title.other: The file carries an edit history with {count} recorded steps

finding.authenticity.xmp_history.detail: Adobe applications keep a log of what was done to an image. Its presence means this file was opened and saved in an editor at least once.
finding.authenticity.derived_from.title: This file is recorded as being derived from another image
finding.authenticity.derived_from.detail: The metadata points back at a parent document, which is what an editor writes when it saves a copy rather than the original.
finding.authenticity.modify_date_differs: The file was written at a different time than the photo was taken
The shutter fired at {taken}, but the file records {modified} as its last write. Something re-saved it afterwards.
The image has been cropped since it was taken
The image has been resized since it was taken

The camera recorded {exif_width} × {exif_height}, but the file now holds {real_width} × {real_height} pixels. The Exif block still remembers the original size because whatever changed the picture did not update it.
finding.authenticity.adobe_segment.title: The JPEG was re-encoded by an Adobe encoder
finding.authenticity.adobe_segment.detai: Adobe's JPEG writer stamps a marker that cameras do not. The pixels have been through at least one extra compression cycle.
finding.authenticity.progressive_jpeg.ti: Saved as a progressive JPEG, which cameras do not produce
finding.authenticity.progressive_jpeg.de: Progressive encoding is chosen by web and messaging pipelines to make images appear faster while loading. A camera writes baseline JPEG.
finding.authenticity.no_makernotes.title: Claims to be {device} but the vendor's private data block is gone
finding.authenticity.no_makernotes.detai: Cameras write a proprietary block full of internal settings. Almost nothing preserves it except the original file, so its absence means the file was re-saved — or the camera name was written in by hand.
finding.authenticity.makernotes_intact.t: The {vendor} private metadata block is intact
finding.authenticity.makernotes_intact.d: This is the strongest single sign of an untouched file: editors, messengers and upload pipelines almost always discard this block.
finding.authenticity.no_exif.title: This file carries no camera metadata at all
finding.authenticity.no_exif.detail: Nothing here records a device, a time or a place. That is completely normal for anything downloaded from the web or received through a chat app, and it is also what a deliberate scrub looks like. There is no way to tell those apart from metadata alone.
finding.authenticity.thin_camera_claim.t: Names a camera ({device}) but almost none of the detail a camera writes
finding.authenticity.thin_camera_claim.d: Missing: {missing}. A genuine capture from a modern device records all of these. A handful of tags naming a camera, with the surrounding detail absent, is what hand-written metadata looks like.
The satellite clock and the camera clock are {gap} days apart
The camera says {camera_date}; the GPS receiver, which takes its time from satellites rather than from the phone, says {gps_date}. One of the two has been changed.
finding.privacy.gps_location.title: Exact location is embedded: {where}
finding.privacy.gps_location.detail: Anyone who receives this file can read the coordinates {coords} straight out of it.{accuracy} If this is your home, your workplace, or anywhere you go regularly, that is now known to every recipient.
finding.privacy.gps_detail.title: The location record also includes {extra}
finding.privacy.gps_detail.detail: Beyond the coordinates, the file records which way you were facing and how high you were — enough to work out which window, which floor, or which direction you were travelling.
finding.privacy.place_names.title: The location is also written out in words: {values}
finding.privacy.place_names.detail: These are separate from the GPS coordinates and survive when only the GPS tags are removed.
finding.privacy.identity_tags.title: The file names a person: {tag}
finding.privacy.identity_tags.detail: These fields are usually filled in once, in a camera's setup menu or an editor's preferences, and then quietly attach to every photo afterwards.
finding.privacy.named_people.title: People are named in the metadata: {names}
finding.privacy.named_people.detail: A photo manager has tagged these people by name and written the names into the file. They travel with it to everyone you send it to.

finding.privacy.face_regions.title.one: {count} face detected, with its position recorded
finding.privacy.face_regions.title.other: {count} faces detected, with their positions recorded

finding.privacy.face_regions.detail: The camera stored where in the frame it saw faces. No names are attached, but the count and positions confirm people are in the shot even to someone who never opens the image.

finding.privacy.device_identifiers.title.one: {count} identifier that ties this photo to one specific device
finding.privacy.device_identifiers.title.other: {count} identifiers that tie this photo to one specific device

finding.privacy.device_identifiers.detai: Values like {tag} are stable across photos. Anyone holding two of your pictures can prove they came from the same camera, even if nothing else matches.
finding.privacy.keywords.detail: Keyword lists often describe subjects, events or people, and are added automatically by photo library software.
finding.privacy.timezone.title: The time zone you were in is recorded (UTC{offset})
finding.privacy.timezone.detail: Even with coordinates removed, the offset narrows you to a band of the world, and across several photos it maps out your travel.
finding.privacy.device_uptime.title: Your phone had been switched on for {uptime} when you took this
finding.privacy.device_uptime.detail: This counter resets when the device reboots. Comparing it across photos reveals which ones came from the same session and how they are ordered, regardless of what the timestamps say.
finding.privacy.embedded_thumbnail.title: A small preview image is embedded alongside the full picture
finding.privacy.embedded_thumbnail.detai: Normal for a camera file. It matters only if the image is later cropped by a tool that forgets to regenerate the preview, which would leave the original framing inside the file.
finding.privacy.stale_thumbnail.title: The embedded preview may still show what was cropped out
finding.privacy.stale_thumbnail.detail: This image was resized or cropped after capture, but it still carries a preview thumbnail. Editors that fail to regenerate the preview leave the original framing visible inside the file — this is how redacted photos have leaked what they were hiding. Check it with: exiftool -b -ThumbnailImage photo.jpg > thumb.jpg
finding.structural.trailing_data.title: {size} of data sits after the image officially ends
This {format} finishes at byte {image_end}, but the file runs to {file_size}. Every viewer stops reading at the end marker, so those bytes are invisible when you look at the picture yet travel with the file wherever you send it. This is how archives and other payloads get stapled to images. Look at what is there with:  tail -c {extra} '{filename}' | xxd | head
A small amount of padding follows the image data, which is usually harmless encoder slack.
finding.structural.truncated.title: The file ends before the image structure does
finding.structural.truncated.detail: Walking the file's internal structure ran off the end without reaching a proper end marker. The file is incomplete — a cut-off download or an interrupted copy — or its internal length fields have been tampered with.
finding.structural.multiple_images.title: The file contains {count} complete images, not one
finding.structural.multiple_images.detai: Phones store a second full-size image alongside the first for portrait mode, HDR and depth effects, so this is usually normal. It does mean a second picture is riding along that you may not have looked at: exiftool -b -MPImage2 '{filename}' > second.jpg
finding.structural.type_mismatch.title: Named .{claimed} but the contents are actually {actual}
The bytes say this is {actual} while the filename claims .{claimed}. A file that is not an image at all, wearing an image extension, is a standard delivery trick. Do not open it in anything that acts on its real type.
The bytes say this is {actual} while the filename claims .{claimed}. Most likely someone renamed it. Worth knowing before you feed it to a tool that trusts the extension.
finding.structural.filename_bidi.title: The filename contains text-direction override characters
finding.structural.filename_bidi.detail: Invisible control characters ({codes}) are present. They reverse how the rest of the name is displayed, so a file that shows as 'holiday‮gpj.exe' is really an .exe. There is no legitimate reason for a photo to be named this way.
finding.structural.double_extension.titl: The filename ends in .{extension}, not in an image extension
finding.structural.double_extension.deta: The name is built to look like an image while the operating system sees an executable or script.
finding.structural.filename_control_char: Newlines or other control bytes in a name break naive scripts and can hide the true extension in terminal output.

finding.structural.code_in_metadata.titl.one: Code-like content found in {count} metadata field
finding.structural.code_in_metadata.titl.other: Code-like content found in {count} metadata fields

finding.structural.code_in_metadata.deta: Found: {hits}. Metadata is data, so this cannot run just because you view the image. It matters when the file reaches a server that passes metadata into a shell or a template — the classic route for a web shell hidden in a photo. Treat this file as untrusted input, do not upload it anywhere, and inspect it with: exiftool -a -G1 '{filename}'
finding.structural.oversized_field.title: {tag} holds {size} of text
finding.structural.oversized_field.detai: A field this large is being used as a container rather than a description. Often it is a legitimate editing history; sometimes it is somewhere to put data that should not be there.

finding.structural.encoded_blob.title.one: Long encoded data found in {count} unexpected field
finding.structural.encoded_blob.title.other: Long encoded data found in {count} unexpected fields

finding.structural.encoded_blob.detail: {tags} contains a long unbroken run of base64-like characters. Some applications legitimately stash data this way; it is also how content gets smuggled through a field nobody inspects.
finding.structural.parse_error.title: exiftool could not fully parse this file

finding.structural.parse_warning.title.one: {count} structural warning while reading the metadata
finding.structural.parse_warning.title.other: {count} structural warnings while reading the metadata

finding.structural.parse_warning.detail: {details}. Malformed metadata usually means a buggy editor, but it is also what a hand-crafted file looks like.
finding.structural.pixel_bomb.title: Declares {megapixels} megapixels from only {size}
finding.structural.pixel_bomb.detail: Decoding this would allocate far more memory than the file suggests — roughly {gigabytes} GB uncompressed. That ratio is the signature of a decompression bomb aimed at whatever opens it. findpic only read the header and never decoded the pixels.
finding.ai.declared_source_type.title: The file declares its origin: {source_type}
finding.ai.declared_source_type.detail: This is a standard field that publishers and AI tools use to state how an image was produced. It is a self-declaration — trustworthy when present, meaningless when absent.
finding.ai.source_type_unknown.title: The file declares an unrecognised source type: {value}
finding.ai.source_type_unknown.detail: findpic does not know this value from the IPTC vocabulary.
finding.ai.generator_signature.title: Metadata names an AI image tool: {names}
finding.ai.generator_signature.detail: A generator left its name in the file. This is strong evidence the image was produced or altered by that tool — though the string itself is trivial to write by hand, so it proves intent more than origin.
finding.ai.diffusion_parameters.title: The file contains a full image-generation recipe
finding.ai.diffusion_parameters.detail: The generation parameters — prompt, sampler, seed and model — are stored in the file. This image was created by a diffusion model, and the recipe to reproduce it is right here: {sample}
finding.ai.c2pa_manifest.title: The file carries a Content Credentials (C2PA) manifest
finding.ai.c2pa_manifest.detail: A signed provenance record is attached, describing how the image was made and edited. findpic reads that it exists but does not check the signature — an unverified manifest can be copied from another file. Verify it properly with c2patool: c2patool '{filename}'
finding.ai.cannot_determine.title: Whether this is a real photograph cannot be determined from metadata
finding.ai.cannot_determine.detail: There are no camera tags and no generator markers. An AI image with its metadata removed and a real photo with its metadata removed are identical to any tool that only reads metadata. Deciding this one needs pixel-level analysis, not findpic.
finding.platform.filename_hint.title: The filename is shaped like it came from: {source}
finding.platform.filename_hint.detail: {note} Filenames are trivially changed, so this is a hint, not a fact.
finding.platform.stripped.title.known: Metadata was stripped, and the {longest}px size matches {platforms}
finding.platform.stripped.title.unknown: Metadata was stripped somewhere along the way
finding.platform.stripped.detail: No camera tags, no vendor block, no timestamps. This is exactly what a photo looks like after a messenger or social network re-encoded it for upload — and also exactly what a deliberately scrubbed file looks like. Metadata alone cannot separate the two.
finding.platform.stripped.detail.known: No camera tags, no vendor block, no timestamps. This is exactly what a photo looks like after a messenger or social network re-encoded it for upload — and also exactly what a deliberately scrubbed file looks like. Metadata alone cannot separate the two. Its longest edge is exactly {longest} pixels, a size used by {platforms}, which makes a platform re-encode the more likely story.
finding.platform.camera_and_editor.title: Original camera details survived the trip through {editor}
finding.platform.camera_and_editor.detai: The file still names the {device} that shot it, even though {editor} wrote the current version. Editors usually preserve Exif while replacing the pixels, so the camera information describes the source photo, not necessarily what you are looking at now.
finding.internal.rule_failed.title: Internal check '{name}' could not run
finding.internal.rule_failed.detail: This is a findpic bug, not a problem with your photo. {error}
cli.description: Read a photo's metadata and explain what device made it, when and where, whether it is an untouched original, and what it leaks.
cli.error.no_exiftool: exiftool was not found. Install it with:
cli.error.no_images: No image files found in the given paths.
cli.legend: originality, privacy, structure  →  + good  ~ fair  ! poor  x bad  ? unknown
accuracy.metres: The camera rated the fix accurate to about {value} metres.
finding.authenticity.jpeg_digest.title.e: The compression tables are {software}'s, not a camera's
Every JPEG encoder leaves a fingerprint in its compression tables. This file's fingerprint matches {software}, while the metadata claims a {device}. The picture was re-saved by that program after it left the camera. Estimated quality setting: {quality}.
finding.authenticity.jpeg_digest.title.l: Re-encoded by a general-purpose JPEG library, not by the camera
The compression tables belong to libjpeg, which ImageMagick, Pillow, GIMP and most website upload pipelines use. It proves the pixels were compressed again after the camera wrote them, but it does not say which program did it. Estimated quality setting: {quality}.
